newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Texaco to buy Monterey for $1.1 billion in stock.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Texaco to buy Monterey for $1.1 billion in stock.

text.p: Texaco Inc. said Monday it planned to buy California independent oil producer Monterey Resources Inc. for more than $1.1 billion in a move that will significantly boost the oil giant's output of heavy crude oil.

The acquisition, one of Texaco's largest since it bought Getty Oil in 1984, calls for the nation's third largest oil company to exchange about $21 worth of its stock for each of Monterey's 54.8 million outstanding shares. In addition, it will assume $285 million of Monterey's debt.

Texaco said the acquisition will add 385 million barrels of oil reserves to its U.S. assets and increase its California production by 54,000 barrels a day to 180,000 barrels a day with more gains possible in coming years. Most of Texaco's existing production in California is heavy crude oil.
Monterey's primary holdings are located in California's San Joaquin Valley.

"Gaining Monterey's valuable reserves and talented employees will further enhance Texaco's leadership position in the area of enhanced oil recovery and give us a clear competitive advantage in a region in which we already have significant production and reserves," Texaco Chairman Peter Bijur said in a statement.
Heavy crude oil is more difficult to refine and so priced more cheaply than lighter grades of crude oil.

The deal comes just a few weeks after Santa Fe Energy Resources spun off its 83 percent stake in the independent producer. In June, Monterey announced an agreement to buy McFarland Energy Inc. for $106 million.
Monterey's stock jumped $5.25 to $20.31 on the New York Stock Exchange. Texaco rose 81 cents to $110.81, also on the NYSE.
Wall Street analysts said Texaco has far better technical capabilities than the small independent producer and would probably generate much better returns for the properties.
"Texaco already has critical mass in California. This is a core operation for them," said Michael Young of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Indeed, a top Texaco executive said the company will seek to reduce Monterey's operating costs by 20 to 25 percent. Monterey recently estimated those costs at $3.55 to $3.60 per barrel.

"We're looking at the possibility of 20 to 25 percent lower. We'll be able to merge the two operations very quickly and we expect to see the gains very early," Claire Farley, president of North American production at Texaco, said in a telephone interview.
Farley said technical advances that Texaco has made in heavy crude oil production should ensure solid profits from the new properties.
The move by Texaco, based in White Plains, N.Y., comes amid industry rumors that it may be looking to buy Canadian heavy oil producer Elan Energy Inc.. Texaco declined to comment on the speculation.
"We're looking for potentially other acquisitions in areas where we have a core business, proven core competencies and we see opportunities to expand," Farley said.
